title: CARP: Classification and Organism-Specific Regression of Antimicrobial Peptides
content: Antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery requires both identifying active sequences and estimating their potency against specific pathogens, yet labeled minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) data remain scarce for most organisms. This study investigates how a pretrained protein language model (PLM), ESM-2, can be fine-tuned for both tasks, how label-efficiently the resulting representation transfers to a new pathogen, and what mechanism underlies that transfer. We introduce CARP (Classification And organism-specific Regression for antimicrobial Peptides), in which a shared backbone feeds an AMP classification head and organism-specific MIC regression heads. On Escherichia coli, fine-tuning outperformed frozen embeddings at every model size, and joint training of classification and regression outperformed single-task regression fine-tuning. Freezing the jointly trained backbone and fitting only a new head for Staphylococcus aureus improved the test Pearson correlation from 0.273 to 0.549 with 45 labeled peptides relative to native ESM-2, while leaving existing predictions unchanged. This gain rests on an activity axis shared by the two organisms. With the limited data available, a 650M-parameter backbone offered no advantage over a 150M-parameter one after joint training or in transfer, and the 150M model was therefore adopted as the final CARP. It achieved a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.290 on E. coli and 0.253 on S. aureus, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.972 for AMP classification.
